title: They laughed at it in the West
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: "They laughed at it in the West."
Hyman writes that in Sanhedrin 17b they said that this is R' Yose son of R' Hanina, and that we find it explicitly in Eruvin 48b: "R' Yose son of R' Hanina laughed at it" (at what R' Hiyya taught).
But Hyman gives the opposite in Nazir 42a: "They laughed at it" (regarding the words of R' Yose son of R' Hanina) "in the West."

Hyman lists this expression in Beitzah 14a, Yevamot 88a, and Shevuot 26a — "they laughed at it in the West" — regarding the words of Rav; and in Bava Batra 102b regarding the words of R' Yohanan; and in Bava Batra 16b, Sanhedrin 109b regarding the words of R' Shila; and in Shevuot 34b regarding the words of R' Shimon; and in Zevachim 15a regarding the anonymous Gemara; and in Keritot 4a regarding the words of Rav Sheshet.

Hyman quotes from the book ד״ור (vol. 3, ch. 15): "For the wisdom of Babylonia (as in the generation of Rav Yehuda) did not find favor in the eyes of the Land of Israel, and also others among the sages of Babylonia loathed its casuistic disputations — and indeed they truly scorned and mocked, in the Land of Israel, the 'talmid' [supplied תלמיד; reading unresolved] of the Babylonians that was brought to them by the students who went up from Babylonia" — end of his words; Hyman takes the quoted author’s intent to refer to what they said, "they laughed at it in the West."

Hyman challenges this: But will even a grain of truth be found in his words? Let the reader judge for himself: is it not so that in every place where we find the expression it does not refer at all to the generation of Rav Yehuda, but to the generation of Rav or R' Yohanan or ר״ח and the like, and once this expression is even found regarding Rav Sheshet.
Hyman continues: And as for the expression we find that R' Yirmeya said, "foolish Babylonians," we have already explained it at length in its entry.

notes.text: Hyman’s examples attribute the expression to several different speakers. His polemic, counterexamples and foolish-Babylonians cross-reference are retained.
The book siglum ד״ור, the quotation’s תלמיד/learning reading, the Sheviit34b locator and ר״ח expansion still require their actual texts.

The named William Davidson Sanhedrin 17b text gives an initial mnemonic attribution and then expressly reverses it; its final attribution of ‘they laughed at it in the West’ is to R' Yose son of Hanina. The named Nazir 42a paragraph places the expression after R' Yose son of R' Hanina’s objection, preserving the direction of Hyman’s counterexample. The complete named Eruvin 48b text, nine whole scalars, does not contain the sought laughter/Hiyya/Yose report; that is a bounded edition-and-locator nonmatch, not absence elsewhere or a repair of Hyman’s 48b. In the saved named Shevuot 34b text, the Shimon ruling is followed immediately by the laughter expression. This supports the stated comparison, while Hyman’s supplied שביעית label remains unchanged and held. The book siglum ד״ור, its volume/chapter locator, the supplied תלמיד wording and the siglum ר״ח remain unresolved, with no fresh collation of the quoted book. Hyman’s grain-of-truth question, appeal to the reader, first-person ‘we’, emphatic chronological rebuttal, and ‘foolish Babylonians’ cross-reference remain his polemic, rather than new historical or collective-identity conclusions. Other cited examples have not been freshly collated here. Both existing mixed notes remain verbatim, and all source holds remain.

The printed notice (III, p. 880) cites Shevuot 34b and Zevachim 15a, where the named texts contain Hyman’s Shimon example and the anonymous discussion, respectively. The supplied Hebrew has Shevi’it 34b and Zevachim 16a. The scan and supplied text both cite Eruvin 48b. The named passage begins with R’ Chiyya’s teaching at the end of 47b and names R’ Yose son of R’ Hanina as the one laughing at the start of 48a. Nazir gives the counterexample, where the laughter follows R’ Yose’s own objection. The printed form תלמיד and the abbreviation ר״ח are retained. The work abbreviated ד״ור and the wording quoted from it remain unconfirmed against an external edition.
